prerequisites: Ability to program using the C programming language

learning_outcomes.text: Understand the fundamental principles and concepts of object-oriented programming (OOP) and functional programming.
Know the syntax and features of Java (for object-oriented programming) and Python (as a multi-paradigm language).
Read and understand API documentation as well as third-party commented source code.
Apply program modeling according to the object-oriented programming paradigm using UML.
Write and comment Java code, both by extending existing classes and creating new ones.
Develop Python applications using a multi-paradigm approach.
Apply techniques for identifying and resolving errors both at compile time and runtime (debugging).
Evaluate and interpret different programming techniques and paradigms (procedural, object-oriented, functional), identifying the most suitable approach to solve a given computational problem.
Critically evaluate the quality, readability, and efficiency of their own and others' source code.
Communicate concepts, design choices, and developed IT solutions using appropriate and internationally recognized technical terminology.
Develop the ability to independently consult and explore the official documentation of languages and libraries/APIs.
Autonomously develop the skills necessary to learn new programming languages or frameworks related to the studied paradigms.

syllabus_topics: Module 1 (first semester): Fundamentals of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)
Introduction to the Object-Oriented paradigm: Concepts of class, object, state, behavior, and message passing; the principles of encapsulation and information hiding.
Object-Oriented Modeling: Introduction to UML class diagrams (syntax, as well as association, aggregation, composition, and inheritance relationships).
Inheritance and Polymorphism: Class extension, method overriding and overloading, subtype polymorphism, and the dynamics of late binding.
Abstraction and Code Management: Abstract classes and interfaces.
Generic Data Types: Type parameterization; definition and use of generic classes, interfaces, and methods, parameter constraints and wildcards, type safety, and code reusability.
Abstract Data Types (ADTs) and Collections: Design, usage, and underlying data structures for Lists, Sets, Maps, Trees, and Hash Tables.
Software Robustness: Exception handling, types of exceptions (checked/unchecked), the try-catch-finally mechanism, and the creation of custom exceptions.
Module 2 (second semester): I/O Fundamentals: Byte streams and character streams (InputStream, OutputStream, Reader, and Writer classes).
File Reading and Writing: Using buffers for I/O efficiency (BufferedReader, BufferedWriter) and managing resources via the try-with-resources syntax.
Advanced File and Path Manipulation: Handling text and binary files, overview of packages for file system management (ava.io and java.nio.file).
Object serialization: The concept of persistence, the Serializable interface, and object streams (ObjectInputStream / ObjectOutputStream).
Recursion: Fundamental principles, base and recursive cases, comparison with the iterative approach, and application to data structures.
Introduction to multi-paradigm languages: Transitioning between paradigms and the features of the Python language that support various programming styles.
Fundamentals of functional programming: The concept of functions as first-class citizens, immutability, and side effects avoidance.
Lambda expressions: Syntax, closures, and anonymous functions.
Higher-order functions: Passing and returning functions as arguments (e.g., map, filter, reduce).
Generative functions: Generators, iterators, and lazy evaluation.
Streams: Processing data streams and performing sequential or parallel operations on collections.
assessment_rules: The final examination consists of a practical computer-based test and an oral interview. The practical computer-based test accounts for 50% of the overall evaluation, and the oral interview accounts for 50%. Intermediate assessments are available for attending students; successfully passing both intermediate tests waives the practical computer-based exam and their results contribute 50% each to the final grade if the exam is completed by the last session of the summer period.
